overall_summary: Space and cosmic anomalies featuring extreme planetary conditions and striking sensory paradoxes vastly outperform generic cognitive psychology and brain facts. Videos with durations between 16-21 seconds that challenge basic physics and use high-contrast visual hooks drive the highest views and engagement.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,055 views) and 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (953 views) are the channel's top performers.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on extreme space anomalies, focusing on planets with physics-defying or highly contrasting features.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' achieved 368 views, showing strong audience interest in physical sensations applied to space.
winning_patterns.action: Incorporate sensory descriptions (smell, taste, touch) into cosmic storytelling to make abstract space concepts tangible.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 views) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) consistently fail to gain traction.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from generic cognitive psychology facts unless they can be framed with an intense, high-stakes mystery hook.

next_video.concept: A planet where ice exists at temperatures hotter than a furnace due to immense gravitational pressure.
next_video.opening_direction: Start with a visual of blazing fire burning on a solid block of ice with the voiceover: 'This ice is hotter than a furnace, and it's not melting.'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the planet's gravity is so crushing it forces water into a solid state despite temperatures reaching 800 degrees.
next_video.reason: Capitalizes on the massive success of 'The Planet of Burning Ice' by using a similar high-retention sensory paradox that challenges basic physics.

experiment: Test a 3-part micro-series on 'Planets That Shouldn't Exist' to build viewer retention and encourage playlist-style binge-watching.
